title: Find the River
description: The hushed closing track of Automatic for the People (1992): Michael Stipe follows a river toward acceptance while John Paul Jones's strings swell behind the band. A farewell that became a fan-favorite epitaph.

pops.text: Closing time: this is the final track on Automatic for the People, the last stop on what the band labeled the album's 'ride' side.
Full-band credit: like most R.E.M. songs of the era, it is written by all four members — Bill Berry, Peter Buck, Mike Mills and Michael Stipe.
String royalty: Led Zeppelin's John Paul Jones arranged the strings on this track and several other songs across the album.
The album was a globe-trotting production, cut in Miami, Bearsville, New Orleans, Seattle and the band's hometown base in Athens, Georgia.
Mortality hangs over the whole record: Automatic for the People is R.E.M.'s meditation on aging and loss, and this river journey is its quiet conclusion.
Late single: it was released as the album's sixth and final single, in late 1993 — nearly a year after the album came out.
Chart footnote: the single reached No. 54 in the UK, modest for an album that hit No. 1 there and No. 2 in the US.
The album's odd title was borrowed from the menu-board slogan of Weaver D's, a beloved Athens soul-food restaurant: 'Automatic for the People.'
Second video life: the official clip circulates as the 'Parallel Video Version,' and a separate official lyric video arrived with the album's 25th anniversary edition in 2017.
Epitaph energy: after R.E.M. split in 2011, this song's river imagery made it a go-to soundtrack for tributes and farewells to the band.

title: Beast of Burden
description: The tender soul ballad inside Some Girls (1978): Keith Richards's pleading chorus, two guitars weaving like a conversation, and Mick Jagger promising he'll never be anyone's beast of burden.

pops.text: It's the soul ballad at the heart of Some Girls, the Stones' 1978 comeback smash, recorded in Paris at Pathé Marconi Studios.
Keith's baby: Richards came up with the title and the chorus music, and Jagger filled in verses — a classic Glimmer Twins split shift.
Guitar weaving in action: Keith Richards and Ronnie Wood trade licks so fluidly that fans still argue over who plays which part.
The phrase is ancient: a 'beast of burden' is a working animal like a donkey or ox — Jagger is vowing he won't be put to work in a one-sided love.
Keith sings along: Richards adds the pleading backing harmonies behind Jagger's lead vocal throughout the chorus.
Single success: released as the second single from Some Girls, it reached No. 8 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1978.
Flip it: the B-side of the US single was another Some Girls rocker, 'When the Whip Comes Down.'
No promo film: the band never shot a music video for it in 1978 — the official lyric video on the Stones' channel arrived decades later, in 2023.
Bette Midler took a swing: her 1984 cover, from the album No Frills, reached No. 71 on the Hot 100 — and her video featured a cameo from Jagger himself.
Some Girls itself spent two weeks at No. 1 in the US and became the band's best-selling studio album there.

title: Coconut
description: A breezy, grinning staple from Widespread Panic's debut album Space Wrangler (1988), sung by John Bell with the Athens jam institution at its loosest. This official upload captures it live in Pensacola in 2016.

pops.text: Debut album goods: 'Coconut' comes from Space Wrangler, Widespread Panic's first album, released in 1988 on Landslide Records.
Home-studio origins: the album was recorded in September 1987 at John Keane's studio in the band's hometown of Athens, Georgia.
Delivery legend: rumor in Athens has long held that Col. Bruce Hampton personally delivered the first pressing of the album to the band.
The classic lineup is all here in the writing-era band: John Bell, guitarist Michael Houser, bassist Dave Schools, drummer Todd Nance and percussionist Domingo Ortiz.
Bell takes the mic: frontman John Bell sings lead, delivering the song's sun-baked, tongue-in-cheek travelogue with his trademark grin.
Concert furniture: 'Coconut' has been a setlist regular for decades, surfacing as an opener, a set closer and a breather between the band's heavier jams.
This upload is official: the band's own channel posted this pro-shot performance from Pensacola, Florida, on September 20, 2016, shot and edited by Andy Tennille.
Personnel check on this version: the Pensacola performance features guitarist Jimmy Herring, who joined the band in 2006 after Houser's death in 2002.
Full-album flex: on September 23, 2010, in Atlanta, the band played the entire Space Wrangler album in order — 'Coconut' included — to open the show.
Staying power: Space Wrangler's songs still anchor Panic setlists nearly four decades on, with 'Coconut' among its most durable calling cards.

title: Way Back Home
description: Wilton Felder's soul-jazz shuffle from Old Socks, New Shoes... (1970), the Jazz Crusaders' final album under that name: Joe Sample's gospel-tinted piano, Felder on sax and bass, and a groove built to stay in the live set.

pops.text: Album closer: this is the final track of Old Socks, New Shoes... New Socks, Old Shoes, the 1970 album that closed out the band's Jazz Crusaders era.
Felder's tune: saxophonist Wilton Felder wrote it — the album credit also names Gladys Knight and Johnny Bristol alongside him.
Double duty: Felder plays both tenor saxophone and electric bass on this track, anchoring the groove he also solos over.
Houston roots: the core band — Felder, Joe Sample and Stix Hooper — first played together as students at Phyllis Wheatley High School in Houston.
The front line: trombonist Wayne Henderson and Felder's sax formed the group's signature two-horn sound, with Sample on piano and Hooper on drums.
Studio facts: it was recorded in May 1970 at Wally Heider Studio 3 in Los Angeles and produced by Stewart Levine.
Label hop: the album appeared on Chisa Records, distributed by Motown, and reached shops in July 1970 — a soul label home for a jazz band.
Name change ahead: after this album the group dropped the word 'Jazz' and became simply the Crusaders for the 1970s.
Single too: a mono single edit followed in November 1970, trimming the album version for radio.
Live staple: the band kept it in the set for years — a later live version opens the Crusaders' 1974 album Scratch, recorded at the Roxy.

title: Into the Mystic
description: Van Morrison's sea-going spiritual from Moondance (1970): acoustic guitar, horns answering like a distant foghorn and a sailor's promise to come home. Morrison said the song is simply about being part of the universe.

pops.text: Moondance goods: it sits on Morrison's 1970 album Moondance, recorded at A&R Recording Studios in New York City in late 1969.
Title swap: Morrison first wrote it as 'Into the Misty,' then changed the last word because 'mystic' felt more ethereal to him.
Two lyrics in one: its opening lines work as homophones — 'born' or 'borne' before the wind — and Morrison could not decide which version to send his publisher.
Foghorn meaning flipped: a foghorn usually warns of danger, but here it tells the sailor he is close to home and to the woman waiting there.
In his own words: Morrison has summed the song up as being 'just about being part of the universe.'
Belfast in the sound: critic Johnny Rogan heard the East Belfast shipyards in it, with the saxophone line imitating a foghorn.
Tambourine mystery: the original 1970 LP mix, from December 1969, has a prominent tambourine; later pressings used a January 1970 mix without it.
The quiet mix returned: that first tambourine mix finally reached CD on a 2008 Japanese Moondance remaster and a Rhino vinyl reissue the same year.
Live document: Morrison carried it on stage for his celebrated 1974 live album It's Too Late to Stop Now.
Album peak: Moondance reached No. 29 on the Billboard album chart, the commercial breakthrough Astral Weeks never gave him.

title: Romeo and Juliet
description: Mark Knopfler's lovestruck Romeo, from Making Movies (1980): a chiming National resonator arpeggio, Roy Bittan's piano and a modern Juliet who chose fame over her Romeo. It reached No. 8 in the UK as a 1981 single.

pops.text: Third album: it first appeared on Making Movies, Dire Straits' third studio album, released in October 1980.
Real heartbreak: Knopfler wrote it after his breakup with Holly Beth Vincent, singer of Holly and the Italians.
Fame, not family: unlike Shakespeare's lovers, this Romeo and Juliet are kept apart because Juliet found fame and moved on.
That opening guitar: Knopfler plays the arpeggios on a National Style 'O' resonator — the same guitar pictured on the Brothers in Arms cover.
Open tuning discovery: he has said he stumbled on those famous arpeggio lines while experimenting with an open G tuning on the National.
Borrowed piano: Roy Bittan of Bruce Springsteen's E Street Band plays piano, reworking a lick from his own part on Springsteen's 'Jungleland.'
Studio and producers: it was recorded at New York's Power Station in the summer of 1980, produced by Knopfler with Jimmy Iovine.
Pop allusions: the lyric nods to West Side Story's 'Somewhere' and to the Angels' 1963 hit 'My Boyfriend's Back.'
Chart split: as a January 1981 single it reached No. 8 in the UK and No. 5 in Ireland — but it never charted as a single in the US.
Covered with love: the Killers recorded it at Abbey Road in 2007, and the Indigo Girls had already covered it on their 1992 album Rites of Passage.

title: Touch Me I'm Going to Scream, Pt. 2
description: The eight-minute disco-funk finale of Evil Urges (2008): Jim James coos over a pulsing Omnichord groove that builds into My Morning Jacket's greatest dancefloor slow-burn. The official VEVO clip is pure kaleidoscope.

pops.text: Bookend trick: Evil Urges opens with 'Touch Me I'm Going to Scream, Pt. 1,' a tender guitar ballad — and closes with this, its mirror-image dance epic.
Same title, opposite planets: Pt. 1 whispers; Pt. 2 pulses for eight minutes on a synth groove, with Jim James in full falsetto seduction mode.
Secret weapon: James plays an Omnichord — a quirky Suzuki electronic instrument with a strum plate — which supplies the track's hypnotic chord wash.
TV debut energy: the band performed the song on Late Night with Conan O'Brien in June 2008, days after Evil Urges was released.
Chart high: Evil Urges debuted at No. 9 on the Billboard 200, the band's best showing to that point.
Award nod: the album earned a Grammy nomination for Best Alternative Music Album.
Production team: James co-produced the album with Joe Chiccarelli, known for his work with The Shins and Beck.
Late-night afterlife: the song later turned up on the soundtrack of the 2015 Jake Gyllenhaal film Demolition.
Live, it stretches: concert versions swell well past the album length, and the band has famously segued it into Pink Floyd's 'Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2.'
Louisville roots: for all its cosmic funk, the band remains Jim James's hometown project — My Morning Jacket formed in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1998.

title: A Whole New World
description: The Aladdin end-credits duet that flew to No. 1 in 1993: Alan Menken and Tim Rice's Oscar winner, sung by R&B veterans Peabo Bryson and Regina Belle — still the only Disney animated song to top the Hot 100.

pops.text: Two versions exist: Brad Kane and Lea Salonga sing it in the film; this pop duet by Bryson and Belle plays over the end credits and became the hit single.
The writers: music by Alan Menken, lyrics by Tim Rice, who stepped in after the death of Menken's usual partner, Howard Ashman.
Production polish: the single was produced by Walter Afanasieff, the hitmaker behind Mariah Carey's early ballads.
Released November 5, 1992, as the single from the Aladdin soundtrack — an album that went on to sell millions.
History at No. 1: on March 6, 1993, it reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 — ending Whitney Houston's 14-week run with 'I Will Always Love You.'
A Disney first that still stands: it remains the only song from a Disney animated film ever to top the Hot 100.
Trophy sweep: it won the Academy Award and Golden Globe for Best Original Song, then the Grammy for Song of the Year in 1994.
Deja duet: Bryson had done this before — his 'Beauty and the Beast' duet with Celine Dion was the Disney pop single just one year earlier.
Old partners: Bryson and Belle had already duetted on 'Without You,' the love theme from the 1987 comedy Leonard Part 6.
Reunion magic: in 2019 the pair surprised a Broadway Aladdin audience by singing it together on stage after the show, 27 years on.

title: Cannonball
description: Kim Deal's grunggae bazooka from Last Splash (1993): a harmonica-mic 'check, check,' a bouncing bassline and the loudest quiet-loud chorus of the alternative era. Spike Jonze and Kim Gordon shot the video.

pops.text: Demo name: Kim Deal's original demo was titled 'Grunggae' — her own word for its mix of grunge crunch and reggae bounce.
That opening voice: Deal sings the intro through a harmonica microphone — the distorted 'ahh' and 'check, check' — once owned by her brother.
One-two punch: Last Splash, released August 30, 1993, on 4AD and Elektra, turned the Breeders from a side project into headliners.
Side project no more: Deal started the band while still the Pixies' bassist, first with Tanya Donelly of Throwing Muses.
Twin power: by Last Splash, Kim's twin sister Kelley Deal had joined on guitar — she learned the instrument for the band.
The rhythm section: Josephine Wiggs's bouncing bassline is the song's engine, with Jim Macpherson's drums counting it in.
Chart ride: 'Cannonball' hit No. 2 on Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks, No. 44 on the Hot 100 and No. 40 in the UK.
Video dream team: Spike Jonze and Sonic Youth's Kim Gordon co-directed the video — a cannonball rolling down a street, the band in a garage, Deal singing underwater.
The album went platinum in the US, and 'Cannonball' became the Breeders' signature song for good.
Phish approved: Phish teased the song inside epic 'Tweezer' jams in 1994 and 1995 — a jam-band stamp of cool.

title: Running on Empty
description: Rock's defining road song, recorded live on stage in Maryland in August 1977: Browne and The Section burning bright on fumes, with David Lindley's slide guitar riding shotgun. From the all-new-songs live album of the same name.

pops.text: Recorded live: the title track was cut on stage at Merriweather Post Pavilion in Columbia, Maryland, on August 27, 1977.
A first of its kind: the whole Running on Empty album consists of brand-new songs recorded live — on stage, backstage, in hotel rooms and on the tour bus.
Browne wrote it about the commute: he has said the song began with him driving to the studio every day while making The Pretender, forever low on gas.
Do the math: 'In '69 I was 21' — Browne, born October 9, 1948, turned 21 at the end of 1969, a detail fans love to audit.
Slide masterclass: David Lindley's searing lap-steel and slide guitar is the song's second voice — his solo is a classic of the form.
The band is The Section: Leland Sklar, Danny Kortchmar, Russ Kunkel and Craig Doerge, the LA session elite, with Lindley out front.
Chart run: as a single it peaked at No. 11 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1978.
The album peaked at No. 3, was nominated for the Album of the Year Grammy, and has sold around seven million copies.
Big-screen legs: the song powers Forrest Gump's running years in the 1994 film, introducing it to a new generation.
Browne performed it at his Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction in 2004 — the road song as lifetime-achievement statement.

title: Give Up the Funk (Tear the Roof off the Sucker)
description: Parliament's gold-selling mothership anthem from Mothership Connection (1975): George Clinton, Bootsy Collins and a choir of funkateers demanding the one thing the universe owes them. We wants the funk.

pops.text: Title flip: the album lists it as 'Give Up the Funk (Tear the Roof off the Sucker)'; the 1976 single led with 'Tear the Roof Off the Sucker.'
Writing trio: George Clinton, Bootsy Collins and drummer Jerome Brailey share the songwriting credit.
Home base: it comes from Mothership Connection, released in December 1975 — the album that beamed Clinton's Starchild mythology to Earth.
Bootsy's bass: the rubbery bottom end is Collins, fresh from James Brown's band and already funk's most recognizable bassist.
Brown's horn men defected: saxophonist Maceo Parker and trombonist Fred Wesley, both James Brown alumni, are in the P-Funk horn ranks on this era's records.
Keyboard cosmos: Bernie Worrell's synthesizers give the funk its science-fiction shimmer throughout the track.
Biggest hit: the single reached No. 15 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 5 on the R&B chart in 1976 — Parliament's highest pop placing.
Gold record: it was certified Gold, Parliament's first million-selling single and Casablanca Records' funk breakthrough.
Sampled forever: its chants and grooves have been lifted across hip-hop and R&B for decades — the funk that keeps on giving itself away.
Hall of fame shelf: Mothership Connection was added to the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry in 2011.

title: Human Nature
description: Thriller's dreamiest cut: a Toto demo Quincy Jones rescued and John Bettis finished, floating Jackson's tender vocal over synthesizer starlight. Released as Thriller's fifth single in July 1983, it hit No. 7.

pops.text: A Toto song first: Steve Porcaro of Toto wrote the melody for his young daughter, after a classmate pushed her and she asked him why.
Happy accident: Porcaro's demo cassette found its way to Quincy Jones, who fell for the tune and held it for Thriller.
Enter the lyricist: John Bettis was brought in to finish the words, turning a father's answer into 'tell 'em that it's human nature.'
Porcaro and fellow Toto members David Paich and Steve Lukather all play on the track — synths and guitar steeped in soft-rock gloss.
Fifth single, still huge: released July 3, 1983, it reached No. 7 on the Hot 100 and No. 2 on the Adult Contemporary chart.
Seven for seven: it was one of Thriller's record seven top-10 singles — every single the album produced went top 10.
No 80s video: uniquely among the big Thriller singles, 'Human Nature' had no music video in its own era — the official clip is a modern creation.
Miles Davis approved: the jazz giant covered it on his 1985 album You're Under Arrest, a nod from one innovator to another.
Sample royalty: SWV's 1993 remix 'Right Here (Human Nature)' built itself on this track and rode it to No. 2 in the US.
Jackson called its mood out himself in later years, performing it as Thriller's tender counterweight — the quiet storm at the album's center.

title: End of the Line
description: The supergroup's rolling farewell: Harrison, Lynne, Dylan, Petty and the late Roy Orbison trade verses on a train that keeps moving, closing Traveling Wilburys Vol. 1 (1988). Well, it's all right — even when it rains.

pops.text: Five legends, one band: George Harrison, Jeff Lynne, Bob Dylan, Tom Petty and Roy Orbison — every Wilbury was already a Hall of Famer or future one.
Closing track: it ends Traveling Wilburys Vol. 1, the surprise-hit debut released in October 1988.
Everyone sings: verses rotate through Harrison, Lynne, Orbison and Petty, with Dylan in the mix — a relay race of unmistakable voices.
Written by all five members and produced by Harrison and Lynne, mostly recorded at Dave Stewart's Los Angeles home studio and Harrison's Friar Park.
Tragedy struck weeks later: Orbison died of a heart attack on December 6, 1988, just as the album was taking off.
The empty chair: filmed that December, the video seats Orbison's guitar in a rocking chair when his verse arrives, beside a framed photo of him.
Drummer in disguise: Jim Keltner plays drums throughout but wasn't an official Wilbury — the videos nickname him 'Buster Sidebury.'
Wilbury names: the members hid behind aliases — Orbison was 'Lefty Wilbury,' Harrison 'Nelson Wilbury,' Dylan 'Lucky Wilbury.'
Single life: released in January 1989, it became one of the album's signature tracks; Vol. 1 went triple platinum in the US.
Accidental band: the Wilburys formed when Harrison needed a B-side — 'Handle with Care' came out too good to bury, and an album followed.

title: Synchronicity II
description: Sting's suburban nightmare in 5 minutes: a factory drone's family meltdown cross-cut with something stirring in a Scottish loch, from Synchronicity (1983) — the final Police album and a monster hit.

pops.text: Concept by Jung: 'synchronicity' is Carl Jung's idea of meaningful coincidence — Sting read up via Arthur Koestler's The Roots of Coincidence.
Two stories, one cut: the verses alternate between a miserable suburban family man and a creature rising from a dark Scottish lake — and the two are clearly linked.
Domestic gothic: 'Mother chants her litany of boredom and frustration' — Sting turns the morning commute into a horror movie.
Title-track family: the album also has a 'Synchronicity I' — this sequel, not the opener, became the hit.
Single stats: released in late 1983, it reached No. 16 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 17 in the UK.
Recorded in paradise, strained in person: Synchronicity was cut at AIR Studios on Montserrat with producer Hugh Padgham, even as the band frayed.
Sting wrote much of the album while staying at Goldeneye, Ian Fleming's Jamaican estate — James Bond's birthplace.
Video on the rubble: Godley & Creme directed the clip, parking each band member atop his own tower of junk while wind and debris swirl.
Final album, biggest album: Synchronicity was the Police's fifth and last studio album, spending 17 weeks at No. 1 in the US.
Andy Summers's riff drives it, and Stewart Copeland's drumming threatens to run it off the road — the Police tension, bottled.

title: Damn I Wish I Was Your Lover
description: A debut single with nothing held back: Sophie B. Hawkins's yearning 1992 breakout from Tongues and Tails, a No. 5 hit whose original video MTV banned — so she shot a flannel-and-jeans version and won anyway.

pops.text: Debut thunderbolt: this was Hawkins's first single, the lead release from her debut album Tongues and Tails (1992).
She wrote it herself — a plea to someone stuck in a damaging relationship, sung with total emotional exposure.
Produced by Rick Chertoff and Ralph Schuckett, pairing Hawkins's raw vocal with big early-90s pop-rock polish.
Chart peak: it climbed to No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 — a remarkable debut that stayed on the chart for six months.
Before the solo career, Hawkins played percussion professionally — she even had a brief, famously short stint in Bryan Ferry's orbit.
The banned video: MTV refused the original clip as too erotic, forcing the label to commission a replacement.
The reshoot: the sanctioned second video is black-and-white — Hawkins in torn-sleeve flannel and jeans, fronting a band.
Both versions survive: the original 'banned' video now sits on Hawkins's own channel, and the two cuts have racked up tens of millions of views.
Grammy doors opened: the album's success earned Hawkins a Best New Artist nomination at the 1993 Grammys.
Tongues and Tails went Gold in the US, and its follow-up single 'Right Beside You' kept her on the charts into 1994.
